title: 3.2.8 Lab: greet with a Default Name
description: Write greet(name) so that calling it with no argument greets "friend", using a default parameter, and calling it with a name greets that name. Practice, not graded: the checks call your function.

steps.title: Write greet
steps.instructions: Write a function declaration called greet that takes one parameter, name.

steps.title: Give name a default
steps.instructions: Write the fallback inside the parentheses: name = "friend" (3.2.7). A call with no argument now uses it.

steps.title: Print the greeting
steps.instructions: Inside greet, use console.log to print Hello, then the name, then an exclamation mark, for example Hello, Priya!

steps.title: Call it both ways
steps.instructions: Call greet() with nothing in the parentheses, then greet("Priya"), and compare the two lines.

requirements.title: greet has a default parameter
requirements.description: Code defines greet with a default value written in the parentheses, as name = something. Help: 3.2.7 (Order Matters)
requirements.hint: The default goes inside the parentheses of the definition, like function greet(name = "friend").

requirements.title: greet is called with no argument
requirements.description: Code calls greet() with nothing in the parentheses. Help: 3.2.7 (Order Matters)
requirements.hint: Add a line below the function that calls greet() with empty parentheses.

requirements.title: greet greets the name, or "friend" when there is none
requirements.description: greet() prints Hello, friend! and greet(name) prints Hello, then that name, then an exclamation mark. Help: 3.2.7 (Order Matters)
requirements.hint: A call with no argument leaves name as undefined unless the parameter has a default. Check the default is "friend", and that a name you pass in still wins over it.

aiCheck.rubricTitle: What the AI read in your code
aiCheck.prompt: The student wrote JavaScript for the lab "3.2.8 Lab: greet with a Default Name". The task they were given: Write a function declaration called greet that takes one parameter, name. You cannot run their code: read it and judge what it WOULD do. Judge each criterion by whether the idea is achieved, however the student wrote it. Different variable and function names, template strings, arrow functions, semicolons, spacing, quotes and order are all fine. Do not require any particular structure unless the criterion names one. Mark a criterion missing only when the idea is absent or the code does the opposite. Code inside a comment never runs. Write each note for THIS student's own code: in a not-met note, name the exact line or name in their code that causes the problem (quote at most a few words of it), say in plain words what it does now versus what the criterion needs, and give one concrete next thing to try, but do NOT write the corrected code. In a met note, say in one short phrase what in their code satisfied it. Do not use generic praise.
